title: AI Act — European Commission overview of the regulatory framework for AI (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)
pub: European Commission — Shaping Europe's digital future
author: European Commission

dom.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The Commission accepts the need for selective, risk-sensitive AI deployment and materially extends the cluster’s governance proposition with a concrete regulatory structure: prohibited and high-risk uses, human oversight, traceability, monitoring and incident reporting, while leaving minimal-risk uses largely unrestricted. It does not address the cluster’s productivity, labour or legal-work-redesign evidence directly.
qs: Once an AI system is on the market, authorities are in charge of market surveillance, deployers ensure human oversight and monitoring, and providers have a post-market monitoring system in place.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The Commission directly supports the cluster’s core proposition by presenting differentiated, enforceable safeguards and innovation support as complementary. It also distinguishes enacted application dates from proposed simplification and links delay to the availability of implementation tools such as standards, though it does not empirically establish regulatory effectiveness or resolve contested standards and cross-border divergence.
qs: Together, these measures guarantee safety, fundamental rights and human-centric AI, and strengthen uptake, investment and innovation in AI across the EU.
The Digital Package on Simplification proposes amendments to simplify the AI Act implementation and ensure the rules remain clear, simple, and innovation-friendly.

kp.k: Risk-based regulation targets developers and deployers
kp.d: The Commission’s summary page, rather than the Regulation itself, presents the AI Act as a comprehensive risk-based framework intended to foster trustworthy AI. Its rationale is that opaque AI decisions can obscure unfair disadvantage, including in hiring and public benefits, and that existing legislation does not adequately address AI-specific challenges. These are the Commission’s regulatory rationale and policy claims, not empirical findings about legal-sector outcomes.
qs: The aim of the rules is to foster trustworthy AI in Europe.
For example, it is often not possible to find out why an AI system has made a decision or prediction and taken a particular action.
Although existing legislation provides some protection, it is insufficient to address the specific challenges AI systems may bring.

kp.d: The overview lists harmful manipulation and exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, individual criminal-offence risk assessment or prediction, untargeted facial-image scraping, workplace and educational emotion recognition, biometric categorisation deducing certain protected characteristics, and public-space real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement as prohibited practices. It dates the prohibitions to February 2025 and identifies Commission guidelines on prohibited practices and the AI-system definition as implementation support.
qs: All AI systems considered a clear threat to the safety, livelihoods and rights of people are banned.
The **AI Act prohibits eight practices**, namely:
The prohibitions became effective in February 2025.

kp.k: Justice and employment applications can be high-risk
kp.d: The Commission includes preparation of court rulings and evaluation of evidence reliability among high-risk examples, directly placing certain justice and law-enforcement applications within the framework. Other listed domains include recruitment and worker management, education, critical infrastructure, product safety, essential services, biometrics, migration, asylum and border management. The page classifies specified use cases, rather than declaring all legal AI high-risk.
qs: AI use cases that can pose serious risks to health, safety or fundamental rights are classified as high-risk.
AI tools for employment, management of workers and access to self-employment (e.g. CV-sorting software for recruitment)
AI use-cases in law enforcement that may interfere with people’s fundamental rights (e.g. evaluation of the reliability of evidence)
AI solutions used in the administration of justice and democratic processes (e.g. AI solutions to prepare court rulings)

kp.k: High-risk systems require safeguards before market entry
kp.d: The overview describes pre-market obligations covering risk assessment and mitigation, dataset quality to minimise discrimination, activity logging, compliance documentation, information for deployers, human oversight, and robustness, cybersecurity and accuracy. It states that high-risk rules take effect in August 2026 and August 2027; these are regulatory requirements and scheduled dates, not demonstrated performance improvements.
qs: **High-risk AI systems** are subject to **strict obligations** before they can be put on the market:
high-quality of the datasets feeding the system to minimise risks of discriminatory outcomes
logging of activity to ensure traceability of results
appropriate human oversight measures
The rules for high-risk AI will come into effect in August 2026 and August 2027.

kp.k: Post-market responsibilities span authorities, deployers and providers
kp.d: The page allocates market surveillance to authorities, human oversight and monitoring to deployers, and post-market monitoring systems to providers. Both providers and deployers are described as responsible for reporting serious incidents and malfunctioning, extending compliance beyond initial market entry.
qs: Once an AI system is on the market, authorities are in charge of market surveillance, deployers ensure human oversight and monitoring, and providers have a post-market monitoring system in place.
Providers and deployers will also report serious incidents and malfunctioning.

kp.k: Transparency rules require disclosure of AI interactions and content
kp.d: The Commission describes disclosure obligations intended to let people recognise interactions with machines, including chatbots. Generative-AI providers must make generated content identifiable, while deepfakes and text published to inform the public on matters of public interest require clear, visible labelling. The overview schedules these transparency rules for August 2026.
qs: For instance, when using AI systems such as chatbots, humans should be made aware that they are interacting with a machine so they can take an informed decision.
Moreover, providers of generative AI have to ensure that AI-generated content is identifiable.
On top of that, certain AI-generated content should be clearly and visibly labelled, namely deep fakes and text published with the purpose to inform the public on matters of public interest.
The transparency rules of the AI Act will come into effect in August 2026.

kp.k: Minimal-risk AI receives no additional rules under the Act
kp.d: The Commission states that the Act introduces no rules for AI deemed minimal or no risk and describes the vast majority of currently used EU AI systems as belonging to this category, with video games and spam filters as examples. The overview supplies no quantitative evidence for that prevalence claim.
qs: The AI Act does not introduce rules for AI that is deemed minimal or no risk.
The vast majority of AI systems currently used in the EU fall into this category.
This includes applications such as AI-enabled video games or spam filters.

kp.k: General-purpose models face transparency, copyright and systemic-risk obligations
kp.d: The overview describes general-purpose AI models as foundations for many EU AI systems and identifies capability or widespread use as possible sources of systemic risk. Provider rules cover transparency and copyright, with risk assessment and mitigation for models that may carry systemic risks. It dates GPAI rules to August 2025.
qs: Some of these models could carry systemic risks if they are very capable or widely used.
This includes transparency and copyright-related rules.
For models that may carry systemic risks, providers should assess and mitigate these risks.
The AI Act rules on GPAI became effective in August 2025.

kp.k: GPAI compliance support includes training-data disclosure
kp.d: The Commission reports publishing three instruments in July 2025: guidance clarifying who falls within GPAI obligations, a voluntary expert-developed Code of Practice addressing transparency, copyright, safety and security, and a public training-content summary template. The template calls for training-data sources, including large datasets and top domain names, and processing information intended to support legitimate parties’ exercise of EU-law rights.
qs: In July 2025, the Commission published 3 key instruments to support the responsible development and deployment of GPAI models:

The GPAI Code of Practice is a voluntary compliance tool submitted to the Commission by independent experts, which offers practical guidance to help providers comply with their obligations under the AI Act related to transparency, copyright, and safety & security.
The Template for the public summary of training content of GPAI models requires providers to give an overview of the data used to train their models.
The template also requests information about data processing aspects to enable parties with legitimate interests to exercise their rights under EU law.

kp.k: Further transparency guidance remained under preparation
kp.d: As of the January 2026 update, the Commission was preparing a voluntary code on marking and labelling AI-generated content and guidelines clarifying transparency-rule scope, definitions, obligations, exceptions and horizontal issues. Publication was planned for the second quarter of 2026, distinguishing these prospective instruments from the July 2025 GPAI tools.
qs: The code will be a voluntary tool to guide providers and deployers of generative AI systems to comply with transparency obligations.
The Guidelines on transparent AI systems to clarify the scope of application, relevant legal definitions, the transparency obligations, the exceptions and related horizontal issues.
These support instruments are under preparation and will be published in the second quarter of 2026.

kp.k: Implementation combines European and Member State oversight
kp.d: The overview assigns implementation, supervision and enforcement to the European AI Office and Member State authorities, with the AI Board, Scientific Panel and Advisory Forum providing governance direction and advice. Separately, it describes the AI Pact as a voluntary initiative encouraging providers and deployers to comply with key obligations early.
qs: The European AI Office and authorities of the Member States are responsible for implementing, supervising and enforcing the AI Act.
The AI Board, the Scientific Panel and the Advisory Forum steer and advise the AI Act’s governance.

To facilitate the transition to the new regulatory framework, the Commission has launched the AI Pact, a voluntary initiative that seeks to support the future implementation, engage with stakeholders and invite AI providers and deployers from Europe and beyond to comply with the key obligations of the AI Act ahead of time.

kp.d: The page distinguishes entry into force on 1 August 2024 from general applicability on 2 August 2026. Prohibited practices and AI-literacy obligations applied from 2 February 2025; governance and GPAI obligations from 2 August 2025; high-risk systems embedded in regulated products have a transition period until 2 August 2027. These are the stated application dates, separate from proposed simplification amendments.
qs: The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, and will be fully applicable 2 years later on 2 August 2026, with some exceptions:
prohibited AI practices and AI literacy obligations entered into application from 2 February 2025
the governance rules and the obligations for GPAI models became applicable on 2 August 2025
the rules for high-risk AI systems - embedded into regulated products - have an extended transition period until 2 August 2027

kp.k: Proposed simplification would alter timing and oversight
kp.d: The Commission proposes adjusting the high-risk application timeline to a maximum of 16 months, linking application to implementation support such as standards. Proposed amendments would reinforce AI Office powers and centralise oversight of systems built on GPAI models, extend simplifications for SMEs and SMCs, and clarify interaction with other laws. The page says the legislative proposal was adopted on 19 November and remained under Parliament and Council negotiation, so these are proposals rather than enacted changes.
qs: The Commission proposes to adjust the timeline for the application of high-risk rules to a maximum of 16 months.
This ensures the rules apply when companies have the right support tools to facilitate implementation, such as standards.
Reinforce the AI Office’s powers and centralise oversight of AI systems built on general-purpose AI models, reducing governance fragmentation;
The European Parliament and the Council of the EU are now discussing and negotiating the Digital Omnibus on AI.

kp.k: Proposals retain high-risk training and broaden compliance experimentation
kp.d: The proposed simplification package would require the Commission and Member States to promote AI literacy while retaining training obligations for high-risk deployers. It also proposes broader access to regulatory sandboxes described as being set up from 2028 and expanded possibilities for real-world testing. These are prospective compliance and training measures, not findings about lawyer formation or workforce effects.
qs: Require the Commission and Member States to promote AI literacy and ensure continuous support to companies by building on existing efforts (such as the AI Office’s repository of AI literacy practices, recently revamped), while keeping training obligations for high-risk deployers in place;
Broaden measures in support of compliance so more innovators can benefit from regulatory sandboxes that will be set up as from 2028 and by extending the possibilities for real world testing;

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The European Commission claims that AI offers societal benefits but creates risks of opaque decisions and unfair disadvantage that existing legislation does not adequately address.
pts.d: This is principally a cross-domain regulatory overview, rather than a forecast of legal-sector employment or business models. The Commission identifies difficulties understanding AI decisions as an obstacle to assessing unfair treatment in employment and public benefits. It characterises most current EU AI systems as minimal or no risk.

pts.k: The Commission identifies AI used to prepare court rulings and evaluate evidence as high-risk uses subject to safeguards.
pts.d: The direct connection to legal services is the classification of uses in the administration of justice and law enforcement. The source describes risk assessment, data quality, traceability, documentation, deployer information, human oversight, robustness, cybersecurity and accuracy requirements. It does not claim that all legal AI is high-risk, that judges will be replaced, or that these tools have demonstrated particular performance gains.

pts.k: The Commission presents risk-based regulation as a means to protect rights and trust while supporting AI adoption, investment and innovation.
pts.d: The Commission attributes these benefits to the Act together with the wider policy package. It describes bans for unacceptable-risk practices, strict obligations for high-risk systems, disclosure requirements for transparency risks, and no new rules for minimal- or no-risk AI. The claimed benefits are policy assertions, not measured outcomes reported on the page.

pts.k: The Commission claims disclosure and content identification help preserve informed choice and trust, while general-purpose models require additional safeguards.
pts.d: The page describes notification when people interact with chatbots, identifiability of generative-AI content, and visible labelling for specified content. It states that GPAI models are becoming foundations for many EU AI systems and that very capable or widely used models may present systemic risks. It describes transparency and copyright-related obligations for GPAI providers, with risk assessment and mitigation for models that may carry systemic risks.

pts.k: The Commission claims compliance guidance and proposed simplifications will reduce administrative burdens and fragmentation while supporting innovation.
pts.d: The Commission describes the July 2025 GPAI guidelines, voluntary Code of Practice and training-content summary template as complementary compliance instruments. Separately, it presents proposed timeline adjustments, centralised oversight, documentation simplifications and expanded testing opportunities as implementation improvements. These proposed amendments are not presented as enacted rules: Parliament and Council were still negotiating at the page's update.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is the Commission's institutional account of the Act and implementation instruments, not empirical research on AI's effects.
pts.d: The document is a Commission summary page, not the regulation itself. It names Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, guidance, codes of practice, a training-content template and implementation bodies. Examples such as CV sorting, public-benefit decisions and preparing court rulings illustrate regulatory concerns and scope rather than document observed outcomes. No datasets, benchmarks, quantified impacts, case studies or measured effects on legal-service delivery substantiate the broader claims about trust, innovation or burden reduction.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The page describes phased application from 2024 to 2027, alongside proposed changes still under negotiation as of 27 January 2026.
pts.d: The Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. Prohibitions and AI literacy obligations applied from 2 February 2025; governance and GPAI obligations from 2 August 2025. General application and transparency rules are scheduled for August 2026, with an extended transition to 2 August 2027 for high-risk AI embedded in regulated products. Transparency guidance and a content-marking code are expected in the second quarter of 2026. The Commission separately proposes a high-risk timeline adjustment described as 'a maximum of 16 months', tied to support-tool availability, and sandbox measures from 2028. These proposals should not be conflated with the stated application schedule. The page gives no quantified timeframe for achieving trust or innovation benefits.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The framework affects AI providers and deployers, public authorities and people subject to AI-assisted decisions; justice institutions are one specified high-risk setting.
pts.d: Providers face pre-market compliance and post-market monitoring duties; deployers undertake oversight and monitoring; both report serious incidents and malfunctioning. Authorities supervise and enforce. GPAI providers face transparency, copyright and potentially systemic-risk obligations. Members of the public are intended beneficiaries of protections against harmful practices, discriminatory outcomes and undisclosed AI interactions. Listed settings include employment, education, essential services, migration, law enforcement and justice. SMEs and SMCs are identified as beneficiaries of proposed simplifications. The page makes no specific claims about law-firm staffing, billing, legal-market competition or access-to-justice outcomes.
